title: Unbounded Thread Creation (Missing Thread Pool)
pattern: A loop that accepts incoming network connections or external jobs and spawns an OS thread (`std::thread::spawn`) for each request without capping the total number of concurrently active threads.
why_bad: OS threads are heavy resources, each consuming significant kernel/user-space memory (typically 2-8MB for stack space) and requiring scheduler context switching overhead [477]. Under a burst of traffic, unbounded thread spawning will rapidly exhaust system thread capacity limits (e.g., `/proc/sys/kernel/threads-max`), crashing the process with "can't fork" errors or inducing extreme memory pressure and OOM [393, 395].
detection: Identify loop blocks that invoke `thread::spawn` or `std::thread::Builder::spawn` without consuming from a thread pool or using concurrency limiters like semaphores.
fix: Process tasks using a pre-allocated, bounded thread pool (e.g., using the `threadpool` or `rayon` crates) to restrict maximum thread concurrency [393, 395].
source: Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance*, Chapter 13 (USE Method) & Appendix A / passages [393, 395]; Michael T. Nygard, *Release It!*, Chapter 4 / passage [588].
